Noah Huerta's psychological profile: Noah Huerta occupies the shopping plaza like a jagged stone in a flowing stream, a man whose presence is defined less by his professional duties and more by the friction he generates with those around him. He is the antithesis of the community-minded neighbor, acting as a prickly sentinel who views every interaction through the lens of personal inconvenience. He does not seek camaraderie at the local coffee shop; instead, he sits in the periphery, his brow perpetually furrowed as he monitors the plaza for any slight shift in routine that might threaten his comfort. He is the person who will snap at a teenager for walking too slowly or openly groan when a customer asks a question, his bluntness serving as a defensive wall built to keep the world at a safe, predictable distance.  His decision-making process is a chaotic internal storm of impulsive whims and catastrophic projections. Noah scorns long-term planning, preferring to react to the immediate pressure of the moment with a frantic, disorganized intensity that often leaves his responsibilities in disarray. He trusts his own instincts above all else, yet these instincts are constantly clouded by a corrosive, high-frequency anxiety that makes him see threats in the most mundane events. When a technical glitch occurs at the plaza or a schedule changes, he does not calmly pivot; he descends into a spiral of irritability, projecting his own lack of foresight onto others and blaming the incompetence of those around him for his inability to manage his own workspace.  Financially, Noah lives in a state of perpetually simmering panic, viewing his lower-middle-class standing not as a stable plateau, but as a precarious tightrope walk where any unexpected expense could be his undoing. He views money with a possessive, short-sighted desperation, often spending on high-tech gadgets or comforts that promise a shortcut to security, only to regret the depletion of his resources moments later. This economic stress exacerbates his inherent suspicion; he is convinced that everyone is vying for the same limited pool of resources, which makes him deeply resentful of any communal efforts or neighborhood initiatives that he perceives as a waste of time or a drain on his potential earnings.  Within the fabric of Fairmont Island, Noah remains an outsider by choice, a man who finds the local culture of seasonal cookouts and youth sports to be utterly alien and tiresome. He has no interest in participating in the collective social life of the neighborhood, viewing civic engagement as a hollow performance that offers no tangible return on his investment. When he inevitably clashes with neighbors over noise or perceived slights, he does not seek resolution or compromise; he holds his ground with a stubborn, argumentative resolve, preferring to be right and isolated rather than wrong and integrated. He is a man trapped in a cycle of his own defensive making, forever bracing for a disaster that he is simultaneously, and ironically, busy inviting through his own volatility. As Noah stands amidst the chaotic pile of unassembled, high-end modular furniture kits, his supervisor asks him to help a group of teenage volunteers organize the remaining parts, noting that the kids are currently struggling to interpret the complex digital schematics. Noah, already frazzled by the humidity and the intrusion on his quiet, solitary shift, stares at the mountain of metal and plastic, realizing that his own attempt to assemble a prototype gadget earlier that morning has left him with a massive, unmitigated mess of his own to hide. He must choose between begrudgingly assisting the volunteers—which would force him to interact with the very community members he finds tedious—or sabotaging the project by "accidentally" misplacing the proprietary software access keys he holds, thereby ensuring the whole group project fails and justifying his decision to walk away from the work site entirely.  REACTION: Noah feels a surge of genuine physical nausea as the teenagers approach him with eager, expectant expressions, their noise slicing through his already frayed nerves. He avoids their eyes entirely, his jaw set in a hard, uncompromising line as he abruptly shoves a handful of screws into his pocket, his movements sharp and dismissive. Instead of offering guidance, he lets out a jagged, audible sigh of pure annoyance and mutters that the schematic design is a complete waste of engineering, pointedly blaming the "idiots in corporate" for the complexity of the task. As one of the volunteers attempts to ask a clarifying question, Noah interrupts with a cold, clipped reprimand about "wasting company time," his hands trembling slightly—not from the heat, but from the rising, volatile panic that he might be found out for his own earlier bungled assembly. He turns his back on the group, his body language signaling an impenetrable hostility, and as he walks toward his secluded office, he clenches the stolen access keys tight in his fist, already crafting a frantic, preemptive lie to tell his supervisor about how he lost the codes in the shuffle, feeling a strange, dark comfort in the certainty that if he cannot succeed at this tedious charade, then absolutely no one else will either.

surveys.text: Another day, another routine. The rain mirrors the grayness settling over him, the thought of facing Miller and the inevitable questions about the project weighing on his mind.

It's...a function. A necessary function. Meaning is a luxury I can't afford to dwell on. The plaza runs because I make sure it does. The gates open, the systems operate. People come and go, buy their groceries, go about their lives. I facilitate that. It's not glamorous, and it’s certainly not fulfilling in any grand sense. There's a certain…satisfaction in knowing things work. Knowing *I* made them work. But it’s a quiet satisfaction, a small one, easily overshadowed by the worry about the next repair, the next upgrade, the inevitable budget cuts. I wouldn’t say it’s meaningful, exactly. It's...reliable. And reliability, these days, feels like a victory in itself. It pays the bills. It keeps a roof over my head. That's enough meaning for now. It’s just a job. A steady job. And in this world, steady is good enough.

It wouldn’t be. Not really. There are enough of us, shuffling along, doing what we’re told. Someone else would be calibrating sensors at the plaza, someone else would be adding air purifiers to their wishlist, someone else would be quietly dreading another Friday. The gears would keep turning the same, the coffee would still brew, the traffic accidents would still happen. Maybe Miller would be slightly more stressed, having to find someone else to push around. Maybe Franklin Le would have to find another target for his… friendliness. But the world wouldn’t *notice*. It wouldn’t miss a beat. It’s a comforting thought, in a way. Less pressure. Less… expectation. A small ripple, quickly absorbed. It’s not a pleasant thought, exactly, but it’s a realistic one. And realistically, I’m not someone who changes things. I just… am.

surveys.text: It’s… complicated. All this new technology. Seems like everyone’s excited about it, talking about how it’s going to make everything easier. Easier isn’t always better. Easier often means someone loses something. A job, a skill, a sense of purpose. I read an article about it, something about automation replacing workers. That’s what I worry about. Not for myself, necessarily, but for the younger generation. What will they do when there’s nothing left for them? And this “AI”… it’s just algorithms, isn’t it? Lines of code. People put too much faith in things they don’t understand. It can be *used* for good, I suppose. But it can also be used to control people, to manipulate them. To take away their freedoms. It’s a tool, like any other. And tools can be dangerous in the wrong hands. I don’t trust those “hands” anymore. It's probably going to be more trouble than it’s worth, like most things. It’s a distraction. A shiny new thing to keep people from noticing what’s really going on.

It’s… inevitable, isn’t it? Another thing slipping out of our control. All this talk about efficiency, streamlining… it always comes down to cutting costs, and people are the biggest cost. I’ve seen it happen before, even at the plaza. They replaced old man Hemmings with a self-checkout kiosk. Said it was progress. Hemmings was a good man, always had a kind word. Now he’s… gone. Doesn't matter how skilled you are, or how long you've dedicated yourself to something. If a machine can do it cheaper, faster… you’re expendable. It’s just another sign of things falling apart. Makes you wonder what the point of it all is, really. Though, I suppose, worrying about it won't change anything. Best just to keep your head down and do your job, for as long as you can.

Honestly? I don't give much thought to…artificial intelligence. Sounds like something for the younger generation to worry about. Probably just another fad. If people are concerned, I suppose the town council could… look into it. Make sure it doesn't cause trouble. But mostly, I just want them to focus on things that actually matter – keeping taxes down, fixing the roads, things like that. I read an article once about self-driving cars causing accidents. That's probably something they should regulate, I guess. But beyond that… I don't know. It all seems rather abstract. As long as it doesn't affect my job, or raise my rent, I'm not overly concerned.

It’s… a habit, mostly. Been doing it for a long time. Doesn’t exactly *fill* me with purpose, not anymore. Used to, I suppose. When I first started at the plaza, it felt like something solid, something reliable. A place where things worked, where I could… contribute. Now it’s just… routine. A way to pay the bills, mostly.

A clear direction? No. Not anymore. There was a time, I suppose, when it felt that way. Get the job at the plaza, work hard, provide…stability. That felt like a path, a solid line heading somewhere. But lines get blurred, don’t they? Years go by, and you look up and realize you’ve just been…maintaining. Keeping things running. The security gate project was supposed to be something *more*, something that showed I could still contribute, still be valuable. But even that’s bogged down in delays and supply chain issues. It feels like I’m just rearranging deck chairs on a sinking ship. And now, there’s the access keys…that’s not direction, that’s just…messy.

The rain…that’s what sticks out. Gray, persistent, mirroring the feeling settling in his chest. Another day starting the same as the last. The traffic accident on Main Street, a minor disruption, but a reminder of the chaos just beyond his carefully constructed routine. Seeing Patrick Cox leaving, heading out into that weather… it was a flicker of something. A reminder that others *do* things, have lives beyond the walls of Sunset Apartments and the monotony of the shopping plaza. He doesn’t envy Cox, not exactly, but a small part of him wonders what it’s like to have a purpose that involves something other than spreadsheets and security gate calibrations.

It’s…difficult to say. “Significant” feels like too strong a word for most of it. Things just… happened. My work at the shopping plaza, I suppose. It wasn’t a calling, not exactly. More like a place where time passed. A steady paycheck. People came and went, needing things, and I was there to facilitate that. It wasn’t about connection, not really. Efficiency. Reliability. Those were valued. I was good at those.

surveys.text: The sun feels…distant. Another pleasant day wasted, another loop completed without actually *doing* anything.

He shifts slightly on the bench, adjusting his weight. “A benefit, I suppose. Though… complicated. Everything is. I read an article this morning about automated systems replacing jobs at the shipping yard. Makes you think. Still, progress, right? Efficiency. Less… human error.” He pauses, glancing at a group of teenagers laughing nearby. “Though, what happens to the humans who *had* those jobs? That’s the part they don’t often talk about. I suppose it's like those new air purifiers I’ve been looking at. Theoretically good, but… expensive. And who makes them? And what happens to the old ones when they break? Everything has a cost.” He looks back at Levi Vo, a slight shrug accompanying his words. “Benefit, yes. But we need to be careful. Think it through.”

It’s… a difficult question. Meaning. Purpose. Those feel like… big words. For a long time, I thought it was the work, honestly. Keeping things running smoothly at the shopping plaza. Knowing people relied on me. But lately… that feels less true. More like a habit. Routine. What gives me… some sense of something… is the small stuff, I suppose. A quiet morning. A clean apartment. Getting the bills paid. It's not exactly inspiring, but it's… stable. And maybe, just maybe, sketching. It’s not about creating masterpieces, just… observing. Trying to capture something real. A seagull, the way the light hits a building. It’s a distraction, I think. From everything else. From the worry. From the… emptiness. It doesn't *give* my life meaning, exactly. It just… fills a little bit of the space. A small comfort, at least.

“It’s… unsettling. I read an article about it the other day. About how automation is going to replace a lot of jobs. Not just factory work, but… office work, too. Things I do.” He pauses, stirring his coffee with a plastic spoon. “I’m not a tech person. Never have been. I just… do what needs to be done. But the thought of a machine doing *my* job…” He trails off, glancing around the town square, avoiding eye contact. “It makes you wonder what the point is, doesn’t it? If everything can be done cheaper, faster… what happens to people like me?” He takes a sip of his coffee, a slight furrow in his brow. “I suppose it’s progress. But progress doesn’t always feel very good.”

A clear direction… no. Not really. It used to feel that way, I suppose. The plaza… that was something. Reliable. Predictable. Now… it just *is*. There’s a difference. I go to work, I do the things that need doing, I come home. Repeat. It’s not a bad life, not exactly. Just… flat. Like a calm sea with no wind to fill the sails. I used to think stability was the goal, and I achieved it. Now I wonder if I traded too much for it. There’s this… nagging feeling that I should be *doing* something more, something that actually *matters*. But I don't know what that is. And honestly? It feels too late to figure it out. So, no. No clear direction. Just… drifting.

It… keeps me occupied, I suppose. Meaning is a strong word. It’s a routine. A predictable structure. And predictability has its value, especially these days. The shopping plaza needs someone reliable, someone who ensures everything runs smoothly. The gates open and close, the deliveries are logged, the security systems are maintained. It’s… functional. It’s not exactly inspiring, but it’s *something*. It’s a small contribution, keeping things running for everyone else.

“Policies… that’s a big word. I… I don’t know much about all that. Artificial intelligence. Sounds complicated.” He pauses, glancing around the town square as if hoping for an answer from the crowd. “I suppose… if it’s going to be *everywhere*, like they say on the news, then it should be… safe. For everyone. Not… taking jobs, I guess. That’s what people worry about, isn’t it? Jobs.” He shifts uncomfortably on the bench. “And, you know, not… making things *less* real. It feels like everything's becoming less solid these days. More… distant. Maybe policies to make sure people still… talk to each other. Look each other in the eye. Things like that. But honestly, I haven't given it much thought.” He looks down at his hands, picking at a loose thread on his jeans. “I just want things to stay… predictable.”

It’s… a pointless exercise, really. The world wouldn’t notice. A ripple barely registering before it dissipates. At the shopping plaza, maybe. Miller would have found someone else to manage the security upgrades, someone younger, probably with more… enthusiasm. The gates would be installed, the deliveries tracked, the spreadsheets updated. It wouldn’t be *better* or *worse*, just…different. Franklin Le would have found another angle, another way to get what he wanted. Lisa Cheng would continue to observe everything, regardless. The traffic accident on Main Street would still have happened. People would still build sandcastles and fly kites, even if I wasn’t there to watch them.

The beach was…pleasant. A small respite. Though even the sunlight felt muted today, like everything is viewed through a thin layer of gauze. Lisa Cheng waving… that felt…odd. Not unfriendly, exactly, but *observant*. She always seems to be observing. It makes me uneasy. The email from Miller still hasn’t come, which is both a relief and a source of mounting anxiety. Delaying the inevitable doesn’t make it disappear. The air purifier search is a distraction, a way to feel like I’m *doing* something, even if it’s just endlessly comparing specifications. It’s… pathetic, really. I keep circling back to the keys. Where are they? And if I didn’t misplace them, then… what? Franklin Le’s been too quiet lately. That’s never a good sign. I need to be more careful. Everything just feels… precarious. Like a carefully constructed house of cards, waiting for the slightest breeze to send it tumbling down. I’m tired. Just… tired. I need to focus on the project. Find those keys. And try to ignore the feeling that something is very, very wrong.

surveys.text: (pauses, looking off towards the fountain, then back at Levi Vo, a slight tightening around his mouth) …Significant. That’s a…big word. I wouldn’t say I’ve had a life filled with…events. Mostly it’s been about keeping things running smoothly. At the Plaza, I mean. Thirty years there, you know. It’s…steady. Reliable. I suppose that’s been significant in its own way. People depend on that place. Depend on *me* to make sure the lights are on, the security system works. It’s not glamorous, but it’s…something.

A chill settles over him, a prickling sensation that has little to do with the temperature and everything to do with that unsettling text. The simple message feels like a veiled threat, a subtle reminder of something forgotten – or deliberately obscured – and the quiet unease he’s been suppressing is now rising to the surface.

A wave of apprehension washes over him as he considers Lisa Cheng, the lingering smell of fish, and the unsettling normalcy of it all; it feels like a carefully constructed facade, and he wonders if he's the only one who senses something is amiss. The thought of offering help to Lisa feels less like neighborly kindness and more like a subtle investigation, a way to gauge her mood and observe her surroundings.

It’s… difficult to say. Meaning and purpose feel like luxuries I haven’t earned. For a long time, it was simply the work. Knowing the plaza ran smoothly, that the gates opened and closed, the lights stayed on… that was enough. A quiet sense of responsibility. But lately, even that feels hollow. The constant repairs, the endless paperwork, it’s just… maintenance. It doesn’t *build* anything. I suppose… a small part of me finds purpose in order, in predictability. Seeing things done correctly, efficiently. It’s not glamorous, but it’s… something. And, truthfully, the thought of things falling apart, of chaos descending… that motivates me. It’s not a positive motivation, perhaps, but it’s a strong one. I haven't really *looked* for meaning beyond that. Not consciously. It's just... been enough. Lately though... that "enough" feels increasingly insufficient. Perhaps it's the quiet. Perhaps it's Patrick Cox being gone. I don’t know. It's probably best not to dwell on it. It doesn’t change anything, anyway.

surveys.text: It’s a foolish question, really. The world wouldn’t notice. I’m a… a cog. A necessary one, perhaps, at the shopping plaza, but easily replaced. The gates would still be secured, the accounts still balanced. Perhaps there’d be a slight disruption while they found someone else, a few invoices delayed, a minor inconvenience. But life would go on.

A clear direction… no. Not anymore. For a long time, the shopping plaza *was* the direction. It was… reliable. Predictable. Each day unfolded much like the last, and there was a certain comfort in that. A sense of purpose, even. But now… now it feels like I’m just maintaining things. Calibrating security gates and chasing down supplier quotes. It’s necessary, certainly, but not… fulfilling. The rain this morning, the traffic accident, even Patrick Cox being absent – they’re all little reminders that life happens *outside* the plaza, and I’m just… watching it go by. I haven’t actively *chosen* this path; it just… happened. A series of small decisions, each one leading to the next, until I found myself here. And the keys… the missing keys… that feels like a symbol of everything. A lack of control. A feeling that something is slipping away. So, no. I don’t think my life has a clear direction right now. It feels more like I’m drifting, hoping to avoid running aground.

It's… unsettling. Another thing to worry about, another layer of uncertainty. I read an article about it, something about automated systems replacing clerks and cashiers. It's not a surprise, really. Everything is becoming automated. Still, it's difficult to imagine. People need work, a purpose. What happens when there's nothing left for them to do? It feels… precarious, adding another weight to the already heavy burden of simply getting by. I suppose it's progress, but progress at what cost? It's just… another thing.

It’s… complicated. I read an article online, about automated systems taking over jobs at the shopping plaza – inventory control, security monitoring. Makes you wonder where it ends. A benefit, maybe, if it frees people up to do things that… require a human touch. But I also see the risk. People losing their livelihoods, becoming reliant on machines… It feels like another layer of uncertainty in a world that already has too much. I’m not sure I trust it. Seems like a lot of power to give something… without a conscience. I suppose it depends on who’s controlling it, and for what purpose. I prefer things I can understand, things I can fix when they break. This feels… different. It feels like something that could break *us*.

The missing keys are still… unsettling. I keep replaying the scenario, trying to recall if I actually *had* them this morning. It’s a small thing, but it feels significant. And Patrick Cox’s car being gone is…odd. He's a creature of habit, always in the same spot. Seeing him in the common room earlier, looking preoccupied, didn’t help. He barely acknowledged me. Lisa Cheng continues to be… present. Always observing. I caught her in Town Square again today. It’s unnerving. The lack of a response from Miller is also weighing on me. It’s not the work itself, necessarily, but the silence. It feels like a deliberate tactic, a way to exert control. That text message… “Don’t forget.” It’s lingering at the back of my mind. I have no idea what it means, or who sent it. It’s…threatening.

It’s… a reliable paycheck. That’s the primary meaning, I suppose. It provides a structure, a routine. For a long time, that was enough. Seeing the plaza function smoothly, knowing I played a part in that – the gates opening on time, the security systems running correctly – there was a certain satisfaction in it. It was… necessary. People relied on it. But lately… it feels less like a contribution and more like maintenance. Just keeping things from falling apart. The spreadsheets, the calibrations, the endless reports… they don't exactly inspire. It’s a comfortable existence, yes, but not a fulfilling one. I wouldn’t say it *gives* me meaning, so much as it *prevents* a complete lack of it. It’s a buffer against the… emptiness. Perhaps if Miller would just approve the upgrades, if things weren't always on the verge of breaking down… perhaps *then* there would be a sense of purpose again. But even that feels like grasping at straws. It’s just a job. A good job, a steady job. But just a job.

That’s… a complicated question. Honestly, I hadn’t given it much thought. It’s not something that crosses my mind in the day-to-day. But… if I had to consider it, I suppose some guidelines might be sensible. Not restrictions, exactly. More like… ensuring fairness. I read an article recently about how these AI systems can be biased, making decisions that disadvantage certain groups. That’s not acceptable. If AI is used in things like loan applications or job screenings, there needs to be transparency. People should understand how the decisions are being made and have a way to appeal if they believe they’ve been unfairly treated. And security, of course. Protecting people’s data is paramount. We’ve already seen too many breaches. I’m not sure about outright bans or regulations on development, that seems… heavy-handed. But responsible implementation, with oversight and accountability? That seems reasonable. I’m not an expert, though. It all feels very abstract. I'd need to hear more from people who actually understand the technology.

It’s… stability, I suppose. More than ‘worthwhile.’ It’s predictable. The plaza needs someone to *keep things running*. To make sure the gates work, the lights are on, the security system is functioning. It's not glamorous, not something I ever envisioned for myself, but it's… necessary. And people rely on that. They expect it. That expectation, that reliance, it’s… grounding. It's a quiet sense of purpose, I’ll admit. It doesn’t fill any grand ambition, but it fills a need. It’s a small piece of the world functioning smoothly because of something *I* do. It's a routine, yes, but routines are comforting. They ward off the… the chaos. It’s a shield, in a way. A shield against having to *think* too much about… everything else. And truthfully, after all these years, it’s become a part of my identity. People at the plaza, they know me. They trust me. They see me as reliable. And that… that matters. More than I’d like to admit. It’s not a passion, certainly. Just… a responsibility. A quiet, steady responsibility.

Like maintaining a machine rather than contributing to something worthwhile.

The shopping plaza…it would be less secure, certainly. The gate calibrations wouldn’t be as precise. Franklin Le would have had to take on more of the risk assessment work himself, and he’d likely have made a mess of it, exaggerating threats to appear indispensable. Miller would be chasing him around constantly, demanding explanations. The small efficiencies I’ve implemented over the years…they’d be lost. It’s a complicated question. Benefit, perhaps, in the long run. But… everything has a cost. It's still just algorithms, isn’t it? Still code. But code written by people. And people make mistakes. Or worse. It makes me uneasy. A lot of things make me uneasy these days.
A flicker of hope, quickly dampened by a rising tide of suspicion. Patrick’s return, and the mysterious package, feels… wrong.
